en: Jātaka:
The Seventy Stories,
Kusā Chapter
1. The Kusajātakasutta:
“This kingdom of yours, together with its wealth and its equipment, along with your own life-span and all objects of desire;”
"Mother, rule this kingdom for me;
I shall go where my beloved Pabhāvati is.
"Carry away the great burden with a crooked mind," [he replied].
By day and by night, at the hour of midnight;
go back quickly, O Kusa, to Kusāvatī!
I desire that you, being ugly, should not dwell here.
“I will not go from here to Kusāvatī,
enticed by the beauty of your radiance;
I delight in the lovely abode of Madda.”
Having abandoned my kingdom, I wander the earth, intent on seeing you and utterly bewildered,
lured by the splendor of your beauty.
I do not know the direction, nor from where I have come;
I am intoxicated by you, O deer-eyed one,
clad in golden bark garments.
O you with the beautiful golden girdle and lovely hips,
my desire is indeed for you;
I do not seek sovereignty over the earth.
“It is a marvel, O King, for one who desires what is undesired; you,
O King, desire that which is undesired.”
"You desire what is unlovely as lovely.
"Whether unwillingly or willingly,
the man who obtains what is dear..."
"We praise gain in this case;
lack of gain there is evil.
"You are digging for the essence of stone."
With wood from the *kaṇikāra* tree,
you try to hold back the wind with a net—
you who desire what is undesired.”
“Surely a stone has been placed within your heart,
O lady of gentle appearance,
since I find no pleasure in you.”
Having come from another country,
when the princess looks at me with a frown, [I am filled with fear].
At that time, I was a cook in King Madda’s inner palace;
when they were smiling at me, [they would say:]
The princess looked on;
at that time I was the reed-gatherer,
and Kusa was the king.
“If indeed the word of the fortune-tellers proves true,
you shall never be my husband.”
“Let them cut me into seven pieces!
“If my words, whether spoken by others or by me, are indeed true;”
"You have no husband;
there is another, Kusā, who has the voice of a lion.
"I will have a necklace made for your neck," she said.
Having reached Kusāvatī, O hunchback,
if Pabhāvatī— whose thighs are like the trunk of an elephant— should look upon me.
"O hunchback, having reached Kusāvatī, I shall have a golden neck-ornament made for you, if you,
O one with thighs like an elephant's trunk,"
Pabhāvatī would say:
"O hunchback, having reached Kusāvatī, I shall have a necklace made for your neck."
If you, O lady with thighs like an elephant’s trunk, would warm me with your radiance,
I shall have a necklace fashioned for your neck.
Having reached Kusāvatī, O hunchback,
if she who has thighs like an elephant’s trunk and is radiant should fail to see me.
"O hunchback, having reached Kusāvatī, I shall have a golden neck-ornament made for you, if you,
O lady with thighs like an elephant's trunk,"
“Let her touch me with her hands.
“Surely this princess does not find even the *kusa* grass bitter;”
“O master, she is a hired servant who seeks no wages.
“Surely this cannot be that hunchback;”
One who speaks such evil speech will receive a cutting of the tongue with a well-sharpened blade.
"Do not measure him by his physical form,
for he shines forth by his stature;
do not regard him merely as one of great wealth."
Do what is pleasing and beautiful;
do not ruin her by your appearance,
O lady of radiant splendor.
Having made it very wealthy,
make it beautiful and dear;
do not defile it with outward form.
She shines forth with her ascent;
considering her to be "Mahābālā" (the Greatly Powerful One),
do what is pleasing and dear to her.
Do not seek him by his physical form,
for he shines forth through his stature; do not call him "Great King" merely because of his royal lineage.
Do what is pleasing and beautiful;
do not ruin her with your form,
O lady of radiant splendor, for she is of noble stature.
Addressing him as "Great King," do what is pleasing and agreeable;
do not deceive him by means of your physical form.
"O radiant one, having made yourself like a lion in appearance,
do what is pleasing and beautiful."
Do not seek her by her form,
for she shines forth because of her stature;
having made her voice melodious, [she speaks].
Do what is pleasing to him,
O lovely one; do not deceive him with your beauty,
O lady of radiant splendor.
Having made it the essence of the Bindu,
perform what is beautiful and dear;
do not defile it with form.
O Radiant One, having made yourself known as "Mañjussarā" (Sweet-Voiced),
act in a way that is pleasing and delightful.
Do not seek him by his form,
for he shines forth in his stature; having recognized him by his honey-sweet voice, [do not seek him by his form].
Do what is pleasing and beautiful;
do not ruin her with your form,
O lady of radiant splendor!
Having performed a hundred crafts,
do what is beautiful and pleasing;
do not defile it with outward form.
"Ascend, O radiant one!
Having become a khattiya,
do what is pleasing and delightful."
Do not seek him by his form,
for he shines forth by his stature;
having made him "Kusarāja," [he is known].
“Do what is pleasing and delightful.
“These elephants are steadfast;
all stand here equipped with their armor.”
"In the past, they crushed the rampart and brought this Pabhāvati here.
"Having made seven holes,"
"I shall reveal this power to the khattiyas who have come here to kill me."
The princess Sāmā, dressed in fine silk,
stood there with her eyes filled with tears.
“Surrounded by a host of female servants.
“Surely that face of yours,
once adorned with earrings and reflected upon by the mirrors and silver bowls, [is now lost].”
Beautiful, with lovely eyes, stainless and free from blemish,
she will dwell alone in the forest, abandoned by the kshatriyas.
Surely those dark locks of mine, with their curling tips—
How soft it was, anointed with the essence of sandalwood!
Yet now, in the midst of the crowded charnel ground,
vultures will drag it away with their feet.
Surely those arms of mine— with copper-colored nails,
fine hair, soft, and anointed with the essence of sandalwood—
have been severed and cast away in the forest by the kṣatriyas.
Having seized them, the vulture goes wherever it pleases.
Surely those two arms, which resembled palm trees and were adorned with Kāsī silk and sandalwood paste, [are now gone].
Among these, a jackal will hang from my belly like a young son, a tender offspring, to his mother;
surely he will cling to that broad, well-rounded belly.
The discarded garment, once adorned with golden girdles, now lying in the forest,
the packs of jackals will drag about.
The cranes, the vultures, the jackals,
and whatever other fanged creatures there may be—
they will surely become ageless.
Having eaten Pabhāvati,
if the far-traveling Kshatriyas had carried off my flesh, [I would have been satisfied].
Having requested bones, Mother,
you should burn them on the roadside;
having had fields prepared, Mother...
Plant a *kaṇikāra* tree here;
when it is in bloom at the end of winter, as the cold has passed away, [you will see it].
“Mother, you should dress me in such beautiful colors and radiance.
Then her mother stood up.
A noblewoman of divine appearance,
having seen both a sword and a slaughterhouse within the royal palace of King Madda.
“O Madda, surely with this sword you will slay your daughter, who possesses such beautiful features and a slender waist.”
You will fall from the rank of the kṣatriyas.
You did not follow my word,
O little daughter, though I desired your welfare.
"Today, covered in blood,
you go to the abode of Yama.
Thus does a person come to ruin."
And he falls into greater evil:
he who does not act upon the beneficial words of those who see his true welfare.
And if today you bear a prince of lovely appearance,
a Kshatriya born of Kusa, [then you shall be happy].
Adorned with a golden jeweled girdle,
honored by the circles of your kinsmen—
you do not go to that state of destruction.
Where the drum resounds and the elephant trumpets,
in that auspicious family of kshatriyas—
What indeed could be more pleasant than this?
The horse neighs at the gate,
and the prince cries out.
O auspicious lady of the Khattiya clan,
what indeed could be more blissful than that,
where peacocks and herons cry out?
In a noble clan of Kshatriyas, resounding with the warbling of cuckoos—
what indeed could be more blissful than that?
“Where indeed is that crusher of enemies,
the subduer of foreign realms,
Kusa of lofty wisdom?”
“Whoever shall deliver us from suffering.
“Right here is he who crushes his enemies,
who crushes the kingdoms of others;”
“Wicked one, he who possesses such vast wisdom will slay you all.
“Are you speaking like one who is mad?”
"You speak like one who is blind and foolish;
if Kusa had indeed come here,
how could we not know it?"
“That man Āḷārika,
within the maidens’ quarters,
having made a firm enclosure, [stood there].”
“You wash the pot while bent over.
You are but a braid, a Caṇḍāla woman;
you are not a defiler of the family.”
“How could one born into the Madda clan make a slave her lover?
“I am neither a Veṇī nor a Caṇḍālī;”
Nor am I a defiler of my family;
O Blessed One, you are the son of Okkāka—
do you perhaps think that I am a slave?
“O Blessed One, he who always feeds twenty thousand brahmins—
Okkāka’s son, sir— ”
Do you perhaps think, "You are a slave"?
He for whom twenty thousand elephants are always harnessed—
"O Venerable One, you are the son of Okkāka;
do you perhaps consider yourself a slave?
You who have ten thousand horses..."
"O Blessed One, the son of Okkāka always employs twenty [servants];
do you perhaps think that he considers you a slave?"
For whom twenty thousand chariots are always yoked— O Blessed One,
the son of Okkāka!
Do you perhaps think,
"You are a slave"? He for whom twenty thousand bulls are always yoked—
"O Venerable One, you are the son of Okkāka;
do you perhaps consider yourself a slave?
You who possess a thousand milch cows..."
"O Blessed One, the son of Okkāka always milks twenty [cows];
do you perhaps consider him to be a slave?"
“Truly, it was a misdeed for you, O fool,
that you [tried to deceive] a powerful kshatriya,
a naga, with the color of a frog.”
“Do not speak of this as having reached the edge of a sword.
“O Great King, Bull among Charioteers, forgive us for our transgression.”
"That which you came here knowing in disguise, we did not know.
"For one such as me, that was not a concealment."
Even though I am but an outcaste,
may you alone have confidence in me;
there is no fault in you, O Deva.”
“Go, foolish woman,
and ask forgiveness from King Kusa, who possesses great power; once King Kusa has been asked for forgiveness, [he will grant it].”
"He will grant you your life.
Having heard her father's words,
Pabhāvatī, who possessed the splendor of a goddess, [replied].
He seized by the feet with his head the mighty King Kusa.
"The watches of the night have passed," [he said].
O Lord, without that [divinity],
I bow my head at your feet;
do not be angry with me, O bull among charioteers.
I acknowledge all that to you;
O Great King, listen to me;
nor is it anything unpleasant to you.
I shall do so again. If,
despite my pleading thus,
you will not do as I say, [I shall act].
"Now my father, having killed me,
will establish me among the kṣatriyas.
"Even as you are thus entreating him,"
Why should I not do your bidding?
I am pure toward you, O auspicious lady;
do not fear, Pabhāvati.
I acknowledge all that to you;
listen to me, O princess;
and there is nothing here that is unpleasant to you.
I would do it again, O lady of beautiful hips, for your sake; indeed,
being capable, I shall endure suffering.
“Having slaughtered a great multitude of Maddas,
he is capable of leading them away.
“Let them yoke the horses to the chariot!”
When my mind is concentrated in various ways,
you shall then behold my power as I shatter the hosts of beings.
And there, within the inner palace of King Madda,
they beheld him stretching like a lion.
Stretching out his double-folded arm,
he mounted the back of the elephant and, having caused Pabhāvati to ascend, he departed.
Having entered the battle,
Kusa let out a lion’s roar;
hearing him roar, they [fled].
Just as other animals flee from a lion,
so did the khattiyas scatter,
overcome by fear at the mere sound of the kusa grass.
Elephant-riders,
chariot-fighters, cavalrymen,
and infantrymen cut one another down.
Standing there, terrified by the sound of the *kusa* grass,
he beheld that head of the battle with a joyful mind.
To King Kusa, Devinda gave the Verocana gem; he,
having won that battle, [received it].
Having obtained the Vairocana gem,
the king, mounted upon the back of an elephant,
entered his city and capital.
Having seized them alive and bound those seven kṣatriyas,
he delivered them to his father-in-law.
These beings, O Lord,
are all under your control;
your enemies have been destroyed by you.
"Do as you wish with them:
release them, or kill them. "These beings belong to you alone; [do with them as you please]."
"For these beings are not mine; you alone, O Great King, are ours—
either release them or kill them."
“These seven daughters of yours are as beautiful as celestial maidens;
give one to each of them.”
“Let them be your sons-in-law.
[He replied: “You are the master of all of us—both ourselves and them.”
“O Great King, you yourself give to each of them whatever you wish.
[He gave] one to each one.
Then there was Kusa, whose voice was like a lion’s roar;
at that time, the daughters of King Madda were the wives of those kshatriyas.
Delighted by that gain,
they were thrilled as they heard the lion’s roar;
they drank from their own watering-troughs.
There were seven Khattiyas at that time.
Taking with her Pabhāvati and the beautiful Vairocana gem, she departed.
The mighty King Kusa went to Kusāvatī. There,
he had two charioteers for his single chariot.
As they entered Kusāvatī,
being equal in complexion and form,
they did not outshine one another.
The mother was reunited with her son,
and both husband and wife were together;
at that time, they were all in harmony.
They dwell upon the prosperous earth.
Thus ends the first Jātaka, the Kusajātaka.
